alignments.same: A shabby room is first described by its wallpaper, torn away in great patches.
alignments.differs: Doyle's paper has peeled with damp and frames the killer's writing; Gilman's has been torn off by hands, up to the height of the narrator's own reach.

from.exact: I will follow that pointless pattern to some sort of a conclusion

to.exact: Finally, he examined with his glass the word upon the wall, going over every letter of it with the most minute exactness.

alignments.same: Someone goes over the marks on a wall with minute attention, looking for what they mean.
alignments.differs: Holmes finishes in minutes and reads the word as a blind; the narrator follows the pattern for weeks, reaches no conclusion, and comes to see a woman in it.

from.exact: a long, straight, even smooch, as if it had been rubbed over and over

to.exact: I could read all that in the dust; and I could read that as he walked he grew more and more excited.

alignments.same: Marks on floor and wall record someone pacing a room again and again.
alignments.differs: Holmes reads a stranger's strides and his growing fury; Gilman's narrator puzzles over the smooch, and at the end her own shoulder fits it as she creeps.

question: Holmes reads the marks in a room to find another man; Gilman's narrator reads the paper and finds herself. What makes one reading detection and the other madness?

substitution.note: Usher, Haunted, Canterville, Turn of the Screw and Northanger have strange houses but no torn paper and no one reading marks on a wall; the Rue Morgue reads a ransacked room but not its walls. The rest have neither.

claim: Watson recalls the Study in Scarlet at Holmes's door, and the tale replays its pieces: a man's trade read from his boots and hands, an actor in disguise who slips past Holmes, Watson as chronicler. In 1887 Holmes laughed off the slip and caught his man; here the actor is a woman, and he never gets even.

from.exact: on the inside of your left shoe, just where the firelight strikes it

to.exact: By a man’s finger nails, by his coat-sleeve, by his boot

alignments.same: A man's trade and recent doings are read from his boot, his hands and his dress.
alignments.differs: In 1887 the rule is an unsigned article Watson calls twaddle; now Holmes reads Watson's own boot and doctor's hands, and Watson, trying it, reads only the paper's price.

from.exact: Male costume is nothing new to me.

to.exact: We were the old women to be so taken in.

alignments.same: An actor disguised across age or sex slips past Holmes, and he owns that he was taken in.
alignments.differs: The young man playing an old woman escapes Holmes's pursuit; Irene, as a youth in an ulster, follows Holmes home and bids him good-night at his own door.

from.exact: I am lost without my Boswell.

to.exact: I have all the facts in my journal, and the public shall know them

alignments.same: Watson is the chronicler who will make Holmes's work known.
alignments.differs: In 1887 Watson writes to give Holmes the credit the police took; here Holmes calls for his Boswell, and the record Watson writes is of Holmes beaten.

question: Holmes calls the 1887 slip “a story against myself” and is sure he will be even; after Irene he calls her “the woman.” What has changed in how the stories measure his method?

substitution.note: The Rue Morgue and the Purloined Letter have a reasoner and a narrator but no reading of a trade from boots and hands, no disguised actor who slips past the detective and no chronicler called by name. Canterville has a player of parts but no detective. The rest have none of the three.

claim: Doyle takes over Poe's plot: a royal personage's compromising document, a holder twice waylaid and searched in vain, a detective who pays for a street disturbance to reach the hiding place, a letter left there for the loser. He inverts its ends: the holder is the wronged party, keeps the photograph, and leaves the letter.

from.exact: Twice she has been waylaid.

to.exact: He has been twice waylaid, as if by footpads, and his person rigorously searched under my own inspection

alignments.same: The royal party's hired men have twice waylaid the holder of the document and searched in vain.
alignments.differs: Poe's holder is a Minister who stole the letter from a queen; Doyle's is a woman keeping a photograph of herself with the king who wronged her.

from.exact: everyone in the street was an accomplice

to.exact: The pretended lunatic was a man in my own pay.

alignments.same: The detective pays for a disturbance in the street so the holder's attention goes where he wants it.
alignments.differs: Dupin's musket-shot draws the Minister to the window while he swaps the letter; Holmes's false cry of fire makes Irene run to her hiding place and show it to him.

from.exact: To be left till called for.

to.exact: he is reduced to opening the letter which I left for him in the card-rack

alignments.same: The winner leaves a letter in the hiding place for the loser to open.
alignments.differs: Dupin leaves his for the Minister he has beaten; Irene leaves hers for Holmes, telling him she saw through his disguise and has taken the photograph away.

question: Dupin acts as “a partisan of the lady”; Holmes is hired by the King against the lady, and asks in the end only for her photograph. Whose side is each detective on, and what does each ending make of it?

substitution.note: The Rue Morgue has Dupin and the Prefect but no document, no waylaying and no paid disturbance. The Turn of the Screw has a letter taken from a table but no searches and no street. A Study in Scarlet has a detective's trap but no hidden document. The rest have none of these.

claim: Both tales set a practised player of many parts, who fakes blood with red paint, against Americans in England. The ghost's stolen paints and famous roles fail on a family that will not be frightened; Holmes's painted wound and clergyman fool everyone but Irene, an American-born actress who outplays him in a costume of her own.

from.exact: I had a little moist red paint in the palm of my hand

to.exact: you stole the paints out of my box to try and furbish up that ridiculous blood-stain

alignments.same: A performer fakes blood with red paint to work on the people of a house.
alignments.differs: Holmes's painted wound gets him carried into Briony Lodge and pitied; the ghost's stain turns vermilion and emerald-green, and the family make a joke of it.

from.exact: His expression, his manner, his very soul seemed to vary with every fresh part that he assumed.

to.exact: a rôle in which he had on more than one occasion produced a great effect

alignments.same: The hero keeps a repertory of costumed parts and is proud of the effect they make.
alignments.differs: Holmes's groom and clergyman deceive a whole street; the ghost's famous characters, from Dumb Daniel to Reckless Rupert, meet only butter-slides and pillows.

from.exact: But, you know, I have been trained as an actress myself.

to.exact: He now gave up all hope of ever frightening this rude American family

alignments.same: The old player is beaten by Americans who do not take his performance at face value.
alignments.differs: The Otises beat the ghost by refusing to be his audience; Irene, born in New Jersey, beats Holmes by acting better, following him home in male costume.

question: The Otises defeat the ghost by laughing at his acting; Irene defeats Holmes by acting too. What does each tale make of the old performer when his audience is American?

substitution.note: The Haunted and the Haunters and Usher have spectres but no painted blood and no repertory of parts; A Study in Scarlet has a disguised actor but no fake blood and no Americans outplaying the hero. The rest have neither paint nor parts.

claim: Both tales turn on a thief who takes a treasure by leaving a lookalike in its place, and on a pursuer who must think as the thief thinks. Dupin matches the Minister's mind and swaps a facsimile back. Valentin's reasoning only follows a trail; the priest had swapped the parcels back already, knowing the dodge from a penitent.

from.exact: I had the sense to make a duplicate of the right parcel

to.exact: he produces a letter somewhat similar to the one in question

alignments.same: The thief carries off a treasure by setting a lookalike beside it and taking the real one.
alignments.differs: The Minister's swap works and he holds the letter for months; Flambeau's duplicate had been swapped back by the priest, and his pocket holds paper and sticks of lead.

from.exact: Stray when he strays; stop when he stops; travel as slowly as he.

to.exact: I fashion the expression of my face, as accurately as possible, in accordance with the expression of his

alignments.same: The pursuer copies his quarry's moves or face so as to see what the quarry sees.
alignments.differs: Dupin's copying of the Minister's mind finds the letter; Valentin copies the road of two priests, and the odd things he sees there were left for him by the victim.

from.exact: Instead of going to the right places—banks, police stations, rendezvous—he systematically went to the wrong places

to.exact: They consider only their own ideas of ingenuity

alignments.same: The tale sets a method of search against the police routine of looking where the searcher would look.
alignments.differs: The Prefect searches every place he would have chosen and fails; Valentin, with no clue, goes on purpose to the wrong places, and that is how the priest's trail reaches him.

question: Dupin wins by thinking as the Minister thinks; Father Brown wins because penitents have told him how thieves think. Is the confessional a better school for detection than reasoning?

substitution.note: Only the Purloined Letter has a treasure taken by setting a lookalike beside it and a reasoner who copies his opponent's mind. The Rue Morgue and A Study in Scarlet have reasoners but no swap; A Scandal in Bohemia has a hidden treasure and a staged street scene but no duplicate. The rest have none of the three.

claim: Both tales send a Parisian reasoner through city streets, where a fruiterer's apples start a chain of association and reason feels its way by what is odd. Poe's amateur outthinks the Paris police. Chesterton makes the head of the Paris police the reasoner, and the odd things he follows were laid for him by a priest.

from.exact: I should like to ask you a question in experimental psychology and the association of ideas

to.exact: The larger links of the chain run thus—Chantilly, Orion, Dr. Nichols, Epicurus, Stereotomy, the street stones, the fruiterer.

alignments.same: A fruiterer with his apples, met in the street, becomes a link in a chain of associated ideas the detective reads.
alignments.differs: Dupin reads back from the fruiterer through his friend's unspoken thoughts; Valentin asks the fruiterer to link swapped price-cards with two clergymen, a chain the little priest made on purpose.

from.exact: any oddity that caught the eye of the pursuer might be the same that had caught the eye of the pursued

to.exact: by these deviations from the plane of the ordinary, that reason feels its way

alignments.same: The detective holds that the odd, not the ordinary, is the path to the truth.
alignments.differs: Dupin finds the oddities in the room and the evidence; Valentin, with no clue, wanders after any oddity in the streets, and every one he finds was staged.

from.exact: the head of the Paris police and the most famous investigator of the world

to.exact: The Parisian police, so much extolled for acumen, are cunning, but no more.

alignments.same: The fame of the Paris police is measured against a man outside the force.
alignments.differs: Poe's amateur outthinks the police; Chesterton makes the chief of police the great reasoner, then has him bow to an Essex priest he had pitied.

question: Valentin's chain of oddities was planted by Father Brown; Dupin's chain of thoughts ran in his friend's head. What happens to the detective's reasoning when the clues are made for him?

substitution.note: Only the Rue Morgue has a fruiterer's apples in a chain of association, a rule that reason goes by the odd, and the Paris police measured against an outsider. The Purloined Letter has the Prefect but no fruiterer and no talk of oddity; A Study in Scarlet's 'strangeness with mystery' has no fruiterer and its police are Scotland Yard. The rest have none of the three.

claim: Both tales measure a famous detective against the phrase 'machine', set a clever man in a mild clergyman's dress, and end with the detective outdone by someone he underrated. Irene beats Holmes and escapes. Valentin catches his thief only by a trail the dull priest laid, and he and the thief bow to the priest together.

from.exact: He was not “a thinking machine”; for that is a brainless phrase

to.exact: the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen

alignments.same: The narrator weighs the great detective against the word machine.
alignments.differs: Watson calls Holmes a perfect machine with no room for love; Chesterton's narrator calls the phrase brainless and makes Valentin a thinking man who knows the limits of reason.

from.exact: an actor like Flambeau, dressed as another priest

to.exact: an amiable and simple-minded Nonconformist clergyman

alignments.same: A master of disguise passes as a simple, harmless clergyman to get near a treasure.
alignments.differs: Holmes in clerical dress finds the photograph but Irene sees through him; Flambeau's priest fools the police, but the real priest marks him from the first by a bulge in his sleeve.

from.exact: Let us both bow to our master.

to.exact: the best plans of Mr. Sherlock Holmes were beaten by a woman’s wit

alignments.same: The tale ends with the famous detective owning someone he had underrated as his better.
alignments.differs: Holmes loses the photograph and keeps Irene's picture; Valentin wins his arrest, and the man he pitied as a simpleton is the one he and the thief bow to.

question: Holmes is beaten by a woman, Valentin is led by a priest, and both men had dismissed them. What does each tale say the reasoning machine fails to see?

substitution.note: Only A Scandal in Bohemia calls its detective a reasoning machine, dresses a master of disguise as a simple clergyman and ends with the detective owning a person he underrated. A Study in Scarlet has a disguised actor but no clergyman and no machine; the Rue Morgue and the Purloined Letter have a reasoner who wins. The rest have none of the three.

claim: Hastings names Holmes as his model and, like Watson, comes home invalided from a war, with no family, and falls in with a detective. Watson scoffs at deduction until he sees it work; Hastings boasts a system of his own and misreads every clue. In both tales the police take the public credit.

from.exact: Having no near relations or friends

to.exact: I had neither kith nor kin in England

alignments.same: The narrator is a soldier sent home from the war on sick leave, with no family to go to, who drifts into a detective's company.
alignments.differs: Watson shares lodgings with a stranger to save money; Hastings is a guest at a country house where the crime then happens, and the detective comes from the village.

from.exact: My system is based on his—though of course I have progressed rather further.

to.exact: What ineffable twaddle!

alignments.same: The narrator gives his view of a detective's method before the case begins.
alignments.differs: Watson calls the article on deduction twaddle and learns its author is Holmes; Hastings claims the method as his own improved system, and Poirot's reasoning defeats it at every turn.

from.exact: All the discoveries have been made by Japp, and Japp will take all the credit.

to.exact: the credit of this smart capture belongs entirely to the well-known Scotland Yard officials

alignments.same: The official detectives receive the public credit for the private reasoner's work.
alignments.differs: Holmes's credit is taken from him by the newspapers; Poirot hands it to Japp on purpose, staying in the background so the murderer will not see him coming.

question: Hastings wants to be Sherlock Holmes and turns out a second Watson. What does Christie gain by making her narrator a would-be detective rather than an admiring chronicler?

substitution.note: Only A Study in Scarlet has a narrator invalided home from a war with no family, an article on deduction he scorns, and Scotland Yard taking the credit. A Scandal in Bohemia has Watson and Holmes but none of the three; the rest have no such narrator.

claim: Both tales hide a damning letter in plain view on a mantelpiece, disguised among things of no value, while the police search the house in vain. Dupin finds it by reasoning that a daring man would not hide it at all. Poirot finds it because ornaments he had straightened himself were crooked again.

from.exact: rolling them up into spills he thrusts them hurriedly in amongst the other spills in the vase on the mantle-piece

to.exact: hung dangling by a dirty blue ribbon, from a little brass knob just beneath the middle of the mantel-piece

alignments.same: The letter lies on the mantelpiece among objects like it, made to look worthless.
alignments.differs: The Minister turns the letter and re-seals it as soiled waste and leaves it in a card-rack for months; Inglethorp, caught with it, tears it into strips and rolls them into spills in a hurry.

from.exact: They’ve been in every room in the house—turning things inside out, and upside down.

to.exact: we took our time, and we searched everywhere

alignments.same: The police search the whole house for the paper and do not find it.
alignments.differs: The Prefect's secret search lasts months; Japp's men turn Styles upside down while the family is out, and no one looks in the vase on the dead woman's mantelpiece.

from.exact: if they were already straightened, there would be no need to straighten them again, unless, in the meantime, someone else had touched them

to.exact: the Minister had resorted to the comprehensive and sagacious expedient of not attempting to conceal it at all

alignments.same: The detective works out that the letter is in the most visible place in the room.
alignments.differs: Dupin reasons from the Minister's daring mind before he enters the room; Poirot reasons from his own habit of tidying, which shows him that someone else touched the vases.

question: Dupin's solution comes from reading his opponent's mind, Poirot's from a fussy habit of his own. Which of the two makes the reader feel the clue was fairly there all along?

substitution.note: Only the Purloined Letter hides a letter in plain view on a mantelpiece while the police search the house. A Scandal in Bohemia hides a photograph behind a panel and finds it by a false fire; Northanger Abbey's searched cabinet yields a washing-bill, not a letter in view; the rest have no hidden paper.

claim: Both tales set a foreign reasoner, praised for his method, before a bedroom found fastened on the inside and police who have no method. Dupin proves the fastening false and a beast came in at the window. Poirot learns one door was unbolted and that the killer never needed to enter: the poison was already in her medicine.

from.exact: All the doors had been bolted on the inside.

to.exact: was locked on the inside when the party reached it

alignments.same: The victim's room is broken into and found fastened from within, so it seems no one could have entered.
alignments.differs: Dupin finds a window that only looked nailed, where an ape climbed in; at Styles Cynthia's door was unbolted, and the poison was in the last dose of her tonic.

from.exact: I am disappointed in Japp. He has no method!

to.exact: There is no method in their proceedings, beyond the method of the moment.

alignments.same: The foreign amateur says the official police have no method.
alignments.differs: Dupin despises the Paris police and lets the Prefect sulk; Poirot is Japp's friend, gives him the discoveries and lets him take the credit.

from.exact: He used to say that all good detective work was a mere matter of method.

to.exact: the method—if method there is—by which you have been enabled to fathom my soul in this matter

alignments.same: The narrator dwells on his friend's method as the thing that makes him a detective.
alignments.differs: Poe's narrator is startled when Dupin reads his thoughts and asks for the method; Hastings believes he has learned it and gone further, and never sees what Poirot sees.

question: Poe's locked room is solved by finding a way in; Christie's by showing that no way in was needed. Does the second kind of solution make the first kind of puzzle obsolete?

substitution.note: Only the Rue Morgue has a bedroom found fastened on the inside and a reasoner who says the police have no method. The Purloined Letter's police have too much method and no locked room; A Study in Scarlet's room is open; Jekyll and Hyde's locked cabinet is broken into but the man inside is found, not a riddle of entry.

claim: Both tales turn on a woman in a man's clothes who passes unknown, and on a verdict that a woman's wit ran the game. Irene dresses as a youth to bid Holmes good night and beats him. Miss Howard dresses as Inglethorp to buy poison; Poirot names her the master mind and she is taken.

from.exact: Miss Howard, disguised as Alfred Inglethorp, enters the chemist’s shop

to.exact: Male costume is nothing new to me.

alignments.same: A woman goes out in a man's clothes and is not known for a woman.
alignments.differs: Irene's disguise lets her follow Holmes home and greet him, a free woman's joke; Miss Howard's lets her buy strychnine in another man's name and plant guilt on a third.

from.exact: I am inclined to think that Miss Howard was the master mind in that affair.

to.exact: the best plans of Mr. Sherlock Holmes were beaten by a woman’s wit

alignments.same: The story ends by giving the cleverest plan in it to a woman.
alignments.differs: Holmes is beaten and honours Irene as 'the woman'; Poirot sees through the woman's plan, and her wit is that of a murderer.

question: Irene Adler wins because she is the wronged party; Evelyn Howard loses because she is the murderer. Did the detective story keep room for a clever woman who is neither victim nor villain?

substitution.note: Only A Scandal in Bohemia has a woman in male costume and a verdict that a woman's wit beat the plans. A Study in Scarlet's disguise is a young man playing an old woman; The Blue Cross's is a man dressed as a priest; the rest have no such disguise.

claim: Watson recalls Lestrade's old scorn for the reasoner, and the novel replays pieces of A Study in Scarlet: a man read from a trace he left, the rule that strange details make a case easier, Lestrade at Holmes's side. Now Watson tries the method himself and gets it mostly wrong, and Lestrade comes as a reverent assistant.

from.exact: “I think,” said I, following as far as I could the methods of my companion, “that Dr. Mortimer is a successful, elderly medical man

to.exact: You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive.

alignments.same: The book opens with a man's life and career read from signs he carries, before he explains himself.
alignments.differs: Holmes reads Watson's war service at a glance; in the Hound Watson reads Mortimer's stick, and Holmes shows most of his conclusions are wrong.

from.exact: The more outré and grotesque an incident is the more carefully it deserves to be examined

to.exact: It is a mistake to confound strangeness with mystery.

alignments.same: Holmes explains afterwards that the strangest detail in the case was the one that led him to the truth.
alignments.differs: In the Study the ring left at the scene leads Holmes to the killer; in the Hound a stolen old boot, after a new one, proves the hound is a real dog.

from.exact: I saw at once from the reverential way in which Lestrade gazed at my companion

to.exact: You may be very smart and clever, but the old hound is the best, when all is said and done.

alignments.same: Lestrade of Scotland Yard works beside the amateur reasoner on a murder.
alignments.differs: In the Study Lestrade laughs at Holmes and the police take the credit; in the Hound he arrives with an unsigned warrant at Holmes's call and falls on his face before the hound.

question: Lestrade now reveres Holmes, yet Watson is shown up again. What does the novel gain by making its narrator try Holmes's method and fail on the first page?

substitution.note: Only A Study in Scarlet has Lestrade's scorn, the Afghanistan reading at first meeting and the strangeness-mystery rule. A Scandal in Bohemia reads Watson's boot but has no Lestrade or police; Styles has Japp, not Lestrade; the rest have no police reasoner pair.

claim: Both tales bring a killing that seems beyond human, a beast's trace by the body, and a reasoner who insists the doers were material. Dupin's ape escaped from its owner, an innocent sailor, and killed on its own. Holmes's hound is a weapon: its owner painted it as the family fiend, and the hard part is proving the master guilty.

from.exact: Yet you must admit that the footmark is material.

to.exact: The doers of the deed were material, and escaped materially.

alignments.same: The reasoner sets aside any spirit and holds to the physical trace the killer left.
alignments.differs: Dupin says it to a narrator who never believed in spirits; Holmes says it to a man of science who half believes the family fiend killed his friend.

from.exact: “Mr. Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound!”

to.exact: “Dupin!” I said, completely unnerved; “this hair is most unusual—this is no human hair.”

alignments.same: A trace found near the body shows that an animal, not a man, was at the death.
alignments.differs: Dupin draws the tuft from the dead woman's hand and lets his friend name it; Mortimer finds the prints himself and the old legend has already named the beast.

from.exact: if we were to drag this great dog to the light of day it would not help us in putting a rope round the neck of its master

to.exact: I perfectly well know that you are innocent of the atrocities in the Rue Morgue.

alignments.same: The detective must settle what the beast's owner had to do with the killing.
alignments.differs: Dupin clears the sailor, whose escaped ape killed by itself; Holmes knows the master guilty but can prove nothing until the hound runs down its victim.

question: Poe's beast kills with no one behind it; Doyle's beast is a man's tool. Which version keeps more of the horror once the explanation is given?

substitution.note: Only the Rue Morgue has a reasoner insisting the doers were material, an animal trace by the body and an innocent owner of the beast. Dracula's dog is supernatural with no owner on trial; Moreau's beasts are not traced by a detective; the rest have no animal killer.

claim: In both tales a disguised opponent sees through Holmes and taunts him with his own name, and he owns the hit. A photograph of a couple decides each case. Irene Adler keeps hers and Holmes never gets even. Stapleton's taunt is his last win: Holmes produces the photograph of his marriage and turns his mistress against him.

from.exact: ‘It might interest you to know that you have been driving Mr. Sherlock Holmes.’

to.exact: “Good-night, Mister Sherlock Holmes.”

alignments.same: A disguised opponent who has spotted Holmes's pursuit calls him by his own name as a parting taunt.
alignments.differs: Irene, in a man's dress, says it in passing at his own door; Stapleton, in a false beard, leaves it with the cabman Holmes will trace.

from.exact: “A touch, Watson—an undeniable touch!” said he.

to.exact: how the best plans of Mr. Sherlock Holmes were beaten by a woman’s wit

alignments.same: Holmes admits that an opponent has outplayed him.
alignments.differs: Irene's win is final and Holmes keeps her photograph as a trophy; Stapleton is a foeman worthy of steel, who flees from Holmes into the mire and is lost.

from.exact: Here is a photograph of the couple taken in York four years ago.

to.exact: “We were both in the photograph.”

alignments.same: A photograph of a man and a woman together is the proof of who is bound to whom.
alignments.differs: The King needs Irene's photograph hidden to save his marriage; Holmes shows Laura Lyons the Vandeleurs' photograph so that she will betray Stapleton.

question: Irene Adler is the one opponent Holmes never beats, while Stapleton's best trick is copied from hers. Why does Doyle let the man lose and the woman win?

substitution.note: Only A Scandal in Bohemia has a disguised opponent greeting Holmes by name, Holmes admitting defeat and a couple's photograph as the decisive proof. A Study in Scarlet's disguised accomplice escapes but never names Holmes; Blue Cross and Styles have disguise without the taunt or photograph.

claim: Both narrators, keeping guard in an old country house, see an unknown man stand high against the sky, then watch from a dark empty room at night. The governess's watcher is a dead valet only she can see. Every phantom of Watson's turns out a living man: Holmes dressed as a tourist, a butler signalling food to a convict.

from.exact: I saw the figure of a man upon the tor.

to.exact: He did stand there!—but high up, beyond the lawn and at the very top of the tower

alignments.same: The narrator sees a strange man standing motionless on a height against the sky, who then vanishes.
alignments.differs: The governess's man looks straight at her and turns out to be Quint, who is dead; Watson's figure on the tor is Holmes, who let the moon rise behind him.

from.exact: he looked like any other tourist upon the moor

to.exact: some unscrupulous traveler, curious in old houses, had made his way in unobserved

alignments.same: The stranger who watches the house is taken for, or proves to be, a passing tourist.
alignments.differs: The governess's tourist theory is false and gives way to a ghost; Watson's watcher really is dressed as a tourist, and is his friend.

from.exact: Barrymore was crouching at the window with the candle held against the glass.

to.exact: There were empty rooms at Bly, and it was only a question of choosing the right one.

alignments.same: At night, in an unoccupied room, someone presses to the window to look out at the grounds.
alignments.differs: The governess watches Miles on the lawn staring up at what she cannot see; Barrymore is signalling to the convict, as his wife confesses when they are caught.

question: James leaves the figure on the tower unexplained, Doyle explains every figure on the moor. Does the Hound lose its terror when the man on the tor is Holmes?

substitution.note: Only The Turn of the Screw has a stranger on a tower seen by the narrator, a traveler theory for him and a night watch from an empty room. Dracula has a figure on a height but no watcher from an empty room; Usher and the Haunted and the Haunters have no stranger seen outside.

claim: Both tales bring newcomers from America to an old English house whose family spectre takes a black dog's shape and frightens its victims out of their wits. The Otises' patent cures cannot stop a ghost that is real, but their children's counterfeit one routs it. At Baskerville the spectre is the counterfeit, a real dog painted with phosphorus to kill.

from.exact: the one frightened to death by the very sight of a beast which he thought to be supernatural

to.exact: began at once to make preparations for turning himself into a large black dog, an accomplishment for which he was justly renowned

alignments.same: The family apparition takes the form of a black dog and has already scared a member of the family out of his health or wits.
alignments.differs: Sir Simon really changes shape and drove an uncle to idiocy; Sir Charles dies of fright before a dog that only looks infernal.

from.exact: I’ll have a row of electric lamps up here inside of six months

to.exact: Pinkerton's Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will clean it up in no time

alignments.same: The new arrival from America promises that a modern product will clear away the old house's gloom.
alignments.differs: Washington's remover takes off the bloodstain and the ghost repaints it every night; Sir Henry's lamps are only a plan, and the danger waits for him on the moor.

from.exact: This paste in the tin is no doubt the luminous mixture with which the creature was daubed.

to.exact: a white dimity bed-curtain, with a sweeping-brush, a kitchen cleaver, and a hollow turnip

alignments.same: The apparition is found to be made by human hands from household things.
alignments.differs: The twins' turnip ghost is a prank that frightens the real ghost; Stapleton's phosphorus paste turns a dog into the family fiend to frighten one baronet to death and hunt the next.

question: Wilde's spectre is real and comic, Doyle's is false and deadly. Which tale takes the family curse more seriously?

substitution.note: Only The Canterville Ghost has an American family in an old English house, a family spectre that becomes a black dog and a counterfeit ghost made from household things. Dracula's dog is no family spectre; the Haunted and the Haunters has no American newcomers or counterfeit.

claim: Both books send a man of science after a secret the old alchemists held, have its holder refuse to tell an ardent seeker for fear of his destruction, and show a giant driving beasts across an unvisited waste. Victor's knowledge destroys him. Verne's professor follows the alchemist's road, flees the giant, and comes home the happiest of learned men.

from.exact: Avicenna, Bacon, Lully, Paracelsus, were the true, the only learned men of the day.

to.exact: I little expected in this enlightened and scientific age to find a disciple of Albertus Magnus and Paracelsus.

alignments.same: Paracelsus and the other alchemists are named as the source of the hidden knowledge that starts the quest, and a modern professor passes judgement on them.
alignments.differs: Krempe calls them musty, exploded systems and Victor must begin anew; Hardwigg calls them the only learned men, and the alchemist's message proves a true road.

from.exact: He would not only rush, himself, to destruction, but drag me with him.

to.exact: I will not lead you on, unguarded and ardent as I then was, to your destruction and infallible misery.

alignments.same: The one who holds a dread secret refuses to tell it to an ardent seeker, because it would lead him to destruction.
alignments.differs: Victor keeps his secret from Walton to the end; Harry gives his up to his uncle after a day without food, and it leads them down and home again.

from.exact: but a giant capable of guiding and driving these prodigious monsters

to.exact: a being which had the shape of a man, but apparently of gigantic stature, sat in the sledge, and guided the dogs

alignments.same: Explorers in a waste no one has visited glimpse, a quarter or half a mile off, a gigantic manlike being driving a team of beasts.
alignments.differs: Walton's giant is Victor's creature, who later speaks to Walton over his maker's body; Harry and his uncle flee, never learn what the giant was, and Harry later reasons him away.

question: Victor warns that the acquirement of knowledge is dangerous; Verne lets his professor come home happy. Is Harry's fear of the secret Victor's lesson, which the novel then proves wrong?

substitution.note: Only Frankenstein has the alchemists Paracelsus and Agrippa as the start of a scientific quest, a secret withheld from an ardent seeker to spare him, and a giant seen driving a team across a waste. Moreau has a man of science and manlike beasts but no alchemists and no withheld secret; Rappaccini and the Birth-Mark have no expedition.

claim: Both tales set a learned man before a puzzle that seems to mix many languages, and end with a gigantic manlike figure named an ape. Dupin holds that truth lies on the surface and proves his ape. Verne's professor misses the surface answer and goes down into the earth; his nephew's ape is a guess to unsee a man.

from.exact: Four different idioms in this absurd phrase.

to.exact: Each is sure that it was not the voice of one of his own countrymen.

alignments.same: A string of sounds or letters seems to hold words from several languages at once, and no one language fits it.
alignments.differs: Dupin reasons that the voice spoke no language because it was an ape's; Saknussemm's letters are plain Latin written backwards, which Harry sees by chance while fanning himself.

from.exact: Oh most cunning Saknussemm; and I to be such a blockhead!

to.exact: Thus there is such a thing as being too profound.

alignments.same: A learned searcher's long, intense working of a problem misses an answer that lay on its surface.
alignments.differs: Dupin finds the surface answer by method where Vidocq errs; Hardwigg's night of algebra is beaten by his nephew's accident, and he then seeks truth in the depths of the earth.

from.exact: of some monkey of the first geological epochs

to.exact: The gigantic stature, the prodigious strength and activity, the wild ferocity, and the imitative propensities of these mammalia are sufficiently well known to all.

alignments.same: A gigantic manlike figure that seems impossible is put down, on the authority of naturalists, as an ape rather than a man.
alignments.differs: Dupin proves his ape by hair, prints and Cuvier, and it is caught; Harry's monkey is a guess made years later to unsee the man he saw, and nothing confirms it.

question: Dupin says truth is found on the mountain-tops, not in the valleys where we seek her. What does Verne's descent find that reasoning on the surface could not, and why does Harry refuse to believe it?

substitution.note: Only the Rue Morgue has a voice that witnesses each take for a different foreign language, the maxim against being too profound, and a gigantic manlike figure settled as an ape from a naturalist's book. The Purloined Letter has the surface answer but no polyglot puzzle or ape; the Hound's beast is a dog, Moreau's beast people are made, not taken for apes.

claim: Both books carry a naturalist from the sea to a master who has quit mankind for an island or ship where he alone is law, and send him home in a small boat with a story none may believe. Nemo's law avenges a lost family and he sobs for it; Moreau's is a beasts' litany, and he owns no remorse.

from.exact: His is the Hand that makes.

to.exact: I am the law, and I am the judge!

alignments.same: Cut off from the world on an island or a ship, one master's will stands as the whole law for everyone around him.
alignments.differs: Nemo names himself law and judge to avenge the country, wife and children he lost; Moreau's Law is a litany his made beasts chant to his Hand, and he takes no interest in it.

from.exact: The study of Nature makes a man at last as remorseless as Nature.

to.exact: Almighty God! enough! enough!

alignments.same: After the narrator has seen what the master's power does to living creatures, he looks in him for remorse.
alignments.differs: Moreau says science has made him remorseless and lectures on pain; Nemo, having sunk a warship with all hands, kneels before his wife's and children's portrait and sobs to God.

from.exact: Neither the captain nor the mate would believe my story

to.exact: Shall I be believed? I do not know.

alignments.same: Escaped in a small boat from the master's domain, the narrator comes back among strangers and asks whether his story will be believed.
alignments.differs: Aronnax shrugs, claims a right to speak of the seas, and hopes Nemo lives on as philosopher; Prendick hides his story to escape being called mad and sees a beast in every face.

question: Nemo leaves mankind to escape its unjust laws, Moreau to escape its squeamishness about pain. Why does Aronnax come home hoping for his master, while Prendick comes home afraid of everyone?

substitution.note: Only Moreau has a naturalist picked up at sea and held by a master who has left mankind for a domain where he is the law, a scene where remorse is denied, and an escape by small boat to disbelief. Dracula's count holds Harker in a castle but is no lawgiver and no escape by sea; Frankenstein's Walton is not held; Journey's professor has not left mankind.

claim: Both voyages turn on a lone savant's own writing, a manuscript meant to outlive him and his initial set where no one else has been, and end as nature hurls the party out and the narrator wakes far away. Saknussemm wrote to guide followers; Nemo writes for no one living, claims the pole for himself, and is left behind.

from.exact: This manuscript, signed with my name, complete with the history of my life, will be shut up in a little floating case.

to.exact: a small scrap of parchment fell out of the leaves

alignments.same: A solitary explorer of a place no one reaches writes down his secret so that chance may carry it to a finder after him.
alignments.differs: Saknussemm's cipher falls out of an old book and starts the voyage; Nemo's case is to be thrown overboard by the last man alive, and the book ends before anyone finds it.

from.exact: Captain Nemo unfurled a black banner, bearing an “N” in gold quartered on its bunting

to.exact: will doubtless find your initials engraved with your own hand upon the centre of the earth

alignments.same: The explorer leaves the letter of his name at a point of the globe no one else has reached.
alignments.differs: Saknussemm carved A. S. along his road for followers, and Hardwigg means to sign beside him; Nemo plants his N to take the pole in his own name, for no follower.

from.exact: My head struck on a piece of iron, and with the violent shock I lost all consciousness.

to.exact: Hans had saved me from death, while I rolled insensible on the flanks of the crater.

alignments.same: The voyage ends when a force of nature throws the party out, the narrator blacks out, and he wakes saved, far from where he expected.
alignments.differs: Harry wakes on a volcano beside his uncle and guide, the expedition whole; Aronnax wakes in a fisherman's hut, cannot tell how he escaped, and never learns whether Nemo lived.

question: Saknussemm writes to be followed; Nemo writes to be read only after all aboard are dead. What does each book make of the man who goes first?

substitution.note: Only Journey has an explorer's written secret found by chance, his initial left at the unreached point, and an ending where nature throws the party out and the narrator wakes far away. Moreau has a found manuscript, but the narrator's, with no initial and a boat escape awake; Dracula and Frankenstein have logs and letters but no explorer's mark.

claim: Both books set a narrator among creatures of human shape who slide back toward the beast, losing strength and wit and turning to flesh. The Eloi and Morlocks fall over ages, from ease and hunger, and the Traveller pities what stays human in them; Moreau's beasts revert in months, and Prendick comes home seeing the beast in every man.

from.exact: They were reverting, and reverting very rapidly.

to.exact: The too-perfect security of the Overworlders had led them to a slow movement of degeneration

alignments.same: The narrator watches beings in human form lose strength, speech and wit, sliding back from man toward the animal.
alignments.differs: The Eloi dwindle slowly over eight hundred thousand years of too much ease; Moreau's Beast Folk lose speech and the upright walk in a few months as the beast-flesh takes back what the knife made.

from.exact: had tasted blood, and gone the way of the Leopard-man

to.exact: The Morlocks at any rate were carnivorous!

alignments.same: The sign that the creatures have fallen from human ways is that they eat flesh, which the narrator learns from a kill he finds.
alignments.differs: On the island the Law forbids flesh and whoever tastes blood becomes a hunted outlaw; below ground no law forbids it, and the meat on the Morlocks' table is the Eloi.

from.exact: I feel as though the animal was surging up through them

to.exact: However great their intellectual degradation, the Eloi had kept too much of the human form not to claim my sympathy

alignments.same: Having seen men degraded, the narrator weighs how much kinship he owes to the degraded.
alignments.differs: The Traveller, far in the future, still sees the human in the Eloi and shares their fear; Prendick, back in London, sees the beast in his fellow men and shrinks from them.

question: The Traveller reads the fall as a punishment of human selfishness; Prendick blames only the stubborn beast-flesh. Does either book think the slide could have been stopped?

substitution.note: Only The Time Machine has a whole people of human shape degraded over time, flesh-eating as the sign of the fall, and a narrator who pities them as kin. Jekyll's Hyde is ape-like but one man and eats no flesh; the Rue Morgue ape and the Hound are beasts, not fallen men; Usher's decaying line keeps its mind; Journey's fossil man and shepherd are men of the past, not degraded.

claim: Both men climb down a shaft into the earth, lose their light in its dark, and find below a manlike keeper of a herd. Verne's depths keep the earth's past alive, its saurians, fossil man and giant shepherd; Wells's underworld holds man's future, pale descendants who keep the other branch of mankind as cattle.

from.exact: I had to clamber down a shaft of perhaps two hundred yards.

to.exact: presented numerous projections which doubtless would assist our descent

alignments.same: The way into the underworld is a well-like shaft, climbed down by holds in its wall.
alignments.differs: Verne's party goes roped together behind a guide; the Traveller goes alone, on bars made for smaller creatures, one bending under him, with Weena crying at the top.

from.exact: Then the match burnt down, and stung my fingers, and fell, a wriggling red spot in the blackness.

to.exact: My lamp, by falling down, had got out of order.

alignments.same: Underground, the explorer's only light gives out and leaves him in total dark.
alignments.differs: Harry's lamp dies while he is lost among bare rock, and the dark itself is the danger; the Traveller's matches burn out among living things, whose hands come at him once the light is gone.

from.exact: These Eloi were mere fatted cattle

to.exact: a giant capable of guiding and driving these prodigious monsters

alignments.same: Under the earth a manlike being keeps a herd.
alignments.differs: Verne's shepherd is a giant of man's oldest past, keeping mastodons, seen far off and fled; Wells's keepers are man's small, pale descendants, and their herd is the other branch of mankind, kept for meat.

question: Verne goes down into the earth's past, Wells forward into man's future, and both find a keeper of cattle below. Why does the past look grander to Verne than the future does to Wells?

substitution.note: Only Journey has a descent by shaft into the earth, a light that fails underground, and a manlike herder found below. Twenty Thousand Leagues goes under the sea by ship, with electric light that never fails; Moreau's ravine dens are dark but no shaft or herd; Usher's vault and Dracula's crypt have no herd and no climb down.
